items.stem: What crises began with the collapse of the US subprime mortgage market and spread worldwide in 2008?
items.answer: The global financial crisis
items.markingKey: The global financial crisis. Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008.

items.stem: A student claims that globalization is a purely economic process. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Globalization has political (international institutions), cultural (media, migration, ideas) and environmental (climate, pollution) dimensions, not only economic ones.
items.markingKey: Globalization has political (international institutions), cultural (media, migration, ideas) and environmental (climate, pollution) dimensions, not only economic ones. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between economic globalization and political globalization.
items.answer: Economic globalization is the integration of markets for goods, services, capital and labour; political globalization is the growth of international institutions, agreements and transnational political networks.
items.markingKey: Economic globalization is the integration of markets for goods, services, capital and labour; political globalization is the growth of international institutions, agreements and transnational political networks. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Taiwan's semiconductor industry (TSMC) as an example, explain interdependence as a source of security.
items.answer: TSMC produces most of the world's most advanced chips, used in phones, cars and weapons systems. global dependence on Taiwanese chips gives many states a stake in Taiwan's security – sometimes called a "silicon shield"
items.markingKey: Context (TSMC produces most of the world's most advanced chips, used in phones, cars and weapons systems.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: global dependence on Taiwanese chips gives many states a stake in Taiwan's security – sometimes called a "silicon shield" – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to interdependence as a source of security.

items.stem: "Interdependence always benefits all countries equally." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Interdependence is often asymmetric: actors that are less dependent gain leverage, and benefits of trade are unevenly distributed within and between countries.
items.markingKey: Interdependence is often asymmetric: actors that are less dependent gain leverage, and benefits of trade are unevenly distributed within and between countries. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Interdependence always benefits all countries equally." Explain why this is inaccurate.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"A cough in Wuhan closed factories in Mexico and emptied supermarket shelves in London within weeks."
— Article on supply chains and the pandemic, 2020 (adapted)

Identify the type of interdependence illustrated and explain it.
items.answer: Economic (supply chain) and health interdependence: a local outbreak quickly disrupted production and consumption across continents, showing sensitivity and vulnerability.
items.markingKey: Economic (supply chain) and health interdependence: a local outbreak quickly disrupted production and consumption across continents, showing sensitivity and vulnerability. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using Keohane and Nye's concepts, analyse the interdependence between the EU and China.
items.answer: Identify multiple channels (trade, investment, students), sensitivity (prices, supply chains), vulnerability (rare earths, EV batteries, EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024), and evaluate whether interdependence promotes cooperation or competition ("de-risking").
items.markingKey: Identify multiple channels (trade, investment, students), sensitivity (prices, supply chains), vulnerability (rare earths, EV batteries, EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024), and evaluate whether interdependence promotes cooperation or competition ("de-risking").

items.stem: Explain why interdependence can be a source of power as well as cooperation.
items.answer: Asymmetric interdependence gives the less dependent actor leverage: e.g. Europe's dependence on Russian gas let Russia cut supplies in 2022, and US control of dollar clearing enables sanctions (weaponised interdependence).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Asymmetric interdependence gives the less dependent actor leverage: e.g. Europe's dependence on Russian gas let Russia cut supplies in 2022, and US control of dollar clearing enables sanctions (weaponised interdependence). items.stem: Classify each example as economic, political, cultural or environmental interdependence: (a) Netflix series watched in 190 countries, (b) EU sanctions coordinated with G7, (c) melting Himalayan glaciers affecting rivers in India and Bangladesh, (d) Apple assembling iPhones in China.
items.answer: (a) cultural; (b) political; (c) environmental; (d) economic. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: (a) cultural; (b) political; (c) environmental; (d) economic. 1 mark each.

items.stem: "Economic interdependence makes war between great powers less likely." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Interdependence raises the costs of war but does not prevent it when leaders prioritise security or nationalism.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: commercial peace theory; costs of disruption (US–China trade); Keohane and Nye's multiple channels. Arguments against: Europe in 1914 was highly interdependent; Russia invaded Ukraine despite trade with the EU; interdependence can be weaponised. Supported judgement: Interdependence raises the costs of war but does not prevent it when leaders prioritise security or nationalism. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The principal judicial organ of the UN, based in The Hague, which settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions"?
items.answer: International Court of Justice

items.stem: Explain the difference between the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.
items.answer: The ICJ is a UN organ that settles disputes between states (e.g. South Africa v Israel, 2023 application); the ICC is a separate treaty-based court that prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression.
items.markingKey: The ICJ is a UN organ that settles disputes between states (e.g. South Africa v Israel, 2023 application); the ICC is a separate treaty-based court that prosecutes individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression. items.stem: A student claims that the UN Secretary-General can order member states to send troops. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The Secretary-General is the chief administrative officer; only the Security Council can authorise force, and troop contributions are voluntary.
items.markingKey: The Secretary-General is the chief administrative officer; only the Security Council can authorise force, and troop contributions are voluntary. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the WHO and COVID-19 and explain what it reveals about the authority of UN specialized agencies.
items.answer: The WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in January 2020; the US announced withdrawal in 2020 (reversed in 2021) and again in January 2025, and a Pandemic Agreement was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2025. the WHO coordinates and advises but depends on state cooperation and funding, so its authority is limited
items.markingKey: Context (The WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in January 2020; the US announced withdrawal in 2020 (reversed in 2021) and again in January 2025, and a Pandemic Agreement was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2025.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Chloé writes: "All UN General Assembly resolutions are legally binding on member states." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: General Assembly resolutions are recommendations except on internal matters such as the budget; only Security Council decisions under Chapter VII bind members.
items.markingKey: General Assembly resolutions are recommendations except on internal matters such as the budget; only Security Council decisions under Chapter VII bind members. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Peacekeepers cannot keep a peace that does not exist. Where there is no political agreement, blue helmets become targets."

items.answer: Peacekeeping relies on a political settlement and consent; without it missions (e.g. MINUSMA in Mali, where over 300 peacekeepers were killed) face attacks and cannot fulfil their mandates.
items.markingKey: Peacekeeping relies on a political settlement and consent; without it missions (e.g. MINUSMA in Mali, where over 300 peacekeepers were killed) face attacks and cannot fulfil their mandates. items.answer: The part of the UN Charter that allows the Security Council to take binding measures, including sanctions and force, in response to threats to peace

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The Charter gave five countries a veto because in 1945 they had won the war. Eighty years later, the world has changed but the Council has not."
— Address by a Global South foreign minister, 2024 (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain why the structure of the Security Council is criticised.
items.answer: The veto and permanent membership reflect the 1945 distribution of power; the rise of new powers and decolonisation mean the Council is unrepresentative, reducing its legitimacy.
items.markingKey: The veto and permanent membership reflect the 1945 distribution of power; the rise of new powers and decolonisation mean the Council is unrepresentative, reducing its legitimacy. items.stem: "The ASEAN system includes a court that can overrule national laws, like the EU Court of Justice." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: ASEAN has no supranational court; it resolves disputes through consultation and consensus, and members retain full sovereignty.
items.markingKey: ASEAN has no supranational court; it resolves disputes through consultation and consensus, and members retain full sovereignty. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "All EU member states use the euro." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Twenty-one of the 27 EU members use the euro (Bulgaria joined in January 2026); others such as Poland, Sweden and Denmark keep national currencies.

items.stem: With reference to ASEAN and the Myanmar crisis, explain how it illustrates the limits of the ASEAN Way.
items.answer: After the 2021 coup ASEAN agreed a Five-Point Consensus, but the junta did not implement it; ASEAN barred Myanmar's junta leaders from summits. non-interference and consensus limited ASEAN to diplomatic pressure, showing weak enforcement capacity
items.markingKey: Context (After the 2021 coup ASEAN agreed a Five-Point Consensus, but the junta did not implement it; ASEAN barred Myanmar's junta leaders from summits.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. "The EU is the only place in the world where 27 democracies have agreed to be overruled by a court and a qualified majority."

items.answer: Members accept binding rulings of the Court of Justice and decisions taken by qualified majority voting in the Council, meaning they can be bound against their will – pooled sovereignty.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a public good and a common-pool resource.
items.answer: A public good is non-rival and non-excludable (e.g. a stable climate, global security); a common-pool resource is non-excludable but rival – one actor's use reduces what is left for others (e.g. fish stocks).

items.stem: Aiko writes: "The backlash against globalization began with the 2016 Brexit vote." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Protests against globalization date back at least to the 1999 Seattle WTO protests; Brexit and the 2016 US election were major expressions of a longer trend.
items.markingKey: Protests against globalization date back at least to the 1999 Seattle WTO protests; Brexit and the 2016 US election were major expressions of a longer trend. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Globalization is a purely economic process." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Globalization has political (international institutions), cultural (media, migration, ideas) and environmental (climate, pollution) dimensions, not only economic ones.
items.markingKey: Globalization has political (international institutions), cultural (media, migration, ideas) and environmental (climate, pollution) dimensions, not only economic ones. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why General Assembly resolutions can matter even though they are generally non-binding.
items.answer: They express the collective view of nearly all states, confer or withhold legitimacy, set norms (UDHR 1948) and can lead to treaties; votes such as ES-11/1 on Ukraine isolate violators diplomatically.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They express the collective view of nearly all states, confer or withhold legitimacy, set norms (UDHR 1948) and can lead to treaties; votes such as ES-11/1 on Ukraine isolate violators diplomatically. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the WTO's consensus-based decision-making has made new trade agreements difficult.
items.answer: With 166 members, any one member can block agreement; the Doha Round launched in 2001 stalled over agriculture and development disputes, so trade liberalisation moved to regional and bilateral deals.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: With 166 members, any one member can block agreement; the Doha Round launched in 2001 stalled over agriculture and development disputes, so trade liberalisation moved to regional and bilateral deals. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why nationalism can limit international cooperation.
items.answer: Nationalist governments prioritise national sovereignty and identity, distrust international institutions as constraints imposed by foreigners or elites, and may withdraw from agreements (e.g. US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and WHO).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Nationalist governments prioritise national sovereignty and identity, distrust international institutions as constraints imposed by foreigners or elites, and may withdraw from agreements (e.g. US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and WHO). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between political globalization and economic globalization.
items.answer: Economic globalization is the integration of markets for goods, services, capital and labour; political globalization is the growth of international institutions, agreements and transnational political networks.
items.markingKey: Economic globalization is the integration of markets for goods, services, capital and labour; political globalization is the growth of international institutions, agreements and transnational political networks. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Zara writes: "The UN Secretary-General can order member states to send troops." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The Secretary-General is the chief administrative officer; only the Security Council can authorise force, and troop contributions are voluntary.
items.markingKey: The Secretary-General is the chief administrative officer; only the Security Council can authorise force, and troop contributions are voluntary. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as an example, explain regional economic cooperation in the Global South.
items.answer: Launched in 2018 and trading since 2021, AfCFTA aims to create a single market across the 54 signatory AU states. African states are pooling trade rules to increase intra-African trade, though implementation is slow
items.markingKey: Context (Launched in 2018 and trading since 2021, AfCFTA aims to create a single market across the 54 signatory AU states.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: African states are pooling trade rules to increase intra-African trade, though implementation is slow – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to regional economic cooperation in the Global South.

items.stem: Briefly describe Brexit and explain what it reveals about backlash against regional integration.
items.answer: The UK voted to leave the EU in 2016 and left in 2020, ending free movement and leaving the single market and customs union. concerns about sovereignty, immigration and identity outweighed the economic benefits of integration for a majority of voters
items.markingKey: Context (The UK voted to leave the EU in 2016 and left in 2020, ending free movement and leaving the single market and customs union.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: concerns about sovereignty, immigration and identity outweighed the economic benefits of integration for a majority of voters – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to backlash against regional integration.

items.stem: With reference to the Red Sea shipping crisis (2023–2024), explain how it illustrates vulnerability of global supply chains.
items.answer: Houthi attacks on ships led major shipping companies to divert around the Cape of Good Hope, raising freight costs and delivery times. a non-state actor in one region raised costs for trade between Asia and Europe, showing how interdependence spreads disruption
items.markingKey: Context (Houthi attacks on ships led major shipping companies to divert around the Cape of Good Hope, raising freight costs and delivery times.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a non-state actor in one region raised costs for trade between Asia and Europe, showing how interdependence spreads disruption – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to vulnerability of global supply chains.

items.stem: With reference to the WHO and COVID-19, explain how it illustrates the authority of UN specialized agencies.
items.answer: The WHO declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in January 2020; the US announced withdrawal in 2020 (reversed in 2021) and again in January 2025, and a Pandemic Agreement was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2025. the WHO coordinates and advises but depends on state cooperation and funding, so its authority is limited

items.stem: A student claims that the ASEAN system includes a court that can overrule national laws, like the EU Court of Justice. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: ASEAN has no supranational court; it resolves disputes through consultation and consensus, and members retain full sovereignty.
items.markingKey: ASEAN has no supranational court; it resolves disputes through consultation and consensus, and members retain full sovereignty. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Suggest two institutional mechanisms that could reduce free-riding in a fisheries agreement and explain one.
items.answer: Monitoring and transparency (satellite tracking, reporting); sanctions or trade measures against violators; quotas with side-payments; reciprocity. E.g. monitoring makes cheating visible so others can respond.
items.markingKey: Monitoring and transparency (satellite tracking, reporting); sanctions or trade measures against violators; quotas with side-payments; reciprocity. E.g. monitoring makes cheating visible so others can respond.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"We discovered in 2022 that our prosperity rested on cheap Russian energy, cheap Chinese goods and American security. Interdependence was not a guarantee of peace but a set of vulnerabilities."
— Speech by a German politician, 2023 (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain how interdependence created vulnerability.
items.answer: Reliance on others for energy, goods and security meant that when Russia invaded Ukraine, Germany faced high costs (energy prices) and limited options; interdependence was asymmetric and could be weaponised.
items.markingKey: Reliance on others for energy, goods and security meant that when Russia invaded Ukraine, Germany faced high costs (energy prices) and limited options; interdependence was asymmetric and could be weaponised. items.stem: To what extent is it true that the United Nations is no longer effective in maintaining international peace and security?
items.answer: The UN is weakest when great powers disagree, but it remains effective in many lower-profile conflicts and as a humanitarian actor.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Security Council paralysis on Ukraine, Syria, Gaza; peacekeeping withdrawals (Mali, DRC drawdown). Arguments against: UN mediation and peacekeeping have ended conflicts (Sierra Leone, Liberia); humanitarian agencies save millions of lives; normative role (GA votes). Supported judgement: The UN is weakest when great powers disagree, but it remains effective in many lower-profile conflicts and as a humanitarian actor. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that regional organizations are more effective than global institutions at promoting cooperation.
items.answer: Regional organizations can achieve deeper cooperation among similar states, but global problems still require global frameworks.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: shared interests and identities (EU single market); AfCFTA, ASEAN trade; regional peace operations (AU in Somalia). items.stem: "Nationalism is the greatest obstacle to international cooperation today." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Nationalism is a major obstacle, but structural collective action problems and great-power rivalry are equally important.
